transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

I’m here because my sleep has just… come apart, I suppose. I’m normally very disciplined about that—early meetings, travel schedules, all of it, you learn not to be sloppy about sleep. But since my cousin died, I keep lying there replaying that night.

And then I’ll finally drift off and wake at 3 or 4 in the morning with these bits of hospital images in my head, not even a whole dream, just scraps. Then I’m sitting in board meetings the next day feeling like I slept in pieces. It’s not like me.
Have you been feeling persistently sad or losing interest in things you usually enjoy since your cousin passed away?

I wouldn’t say I’m crying all day, exactly. I’m still functioning, turning up where I’m supposed to—people expect that of me. But during the prayer gatherings, and even when my nieces tried to comfort me, I found myself doing all the right things, saying the right things… and inside there was just no warmth, no relief.

It’s strange, because I’m usually good with family in those moments. I can be affectionate, practical, both. But it felt like that part of me had gone quiet somehow.
Since your cousin passed away, have you found yourself losing pleasure or interest in activities that you normally enjoy?

Yes… though it’s not so much hobbies, if that makes sense. I’m still doing things, attending what I’m meant to attend. But at the prayer gatherings, and even when my nieces came over trying so hard to comfort me, I could hear myself saying the right words, nodding, touching someone’s hand—very proper, very composed.

And inside there was just… nothing warm. No sense of comfort coming back to me. I kept thinking about how I used to be the one in the family who could make people feel held, you know, and I was also thinking about whether everyone had eaten, whether the tea was being served properly—ridiculous details. But emotionally it was like that affectionate part of me had gone quiet.
Have you noticed a change in your energy level or have you been feeling more fatigued than usual since your cousin passed away?

I’m not sure I’d call it “low energy,” exactly. I mean, I’ve still been getting dressed, going where I’m supposed to go, answering emails—though honestly, some of those emails could have waited, but people send things marked urgent when they really mean “I didn’t plan properly.”

Sorry… fatigue. I suppose I haven’t really measured it that way. I feel worn thin, maybe, but I don’t know if that’s the same as being more fatigued. I’ve just been trying to keep moving.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight since your cousin passed away?

I haven’t really checked, to be honest. People keep putting plates in front of me at the gatherings, and you take a little because otherwise someone notices and makes it a whole conversation.

Weight… I don’t know. My clothes feel about the same, I think. Though I did have to change twice the other morning because nothing seemed appropriate, but that was more about looking presentable than anything else. So no, I haven’t noticed a clear change.
Have you found yourself feeling guilty or blaming yourself for things since your cousin passed away?

Guilty… I don’t know. I mean, everyone always thinks of what they should have done differently after someone dies, don’t they? It’s almost like when there’s a big project at work and afterward everyone says, “Well, if we’d had the meeting earlier,” or “If so-and-so had sent the figures”—not that this is like work, of course, that sounds awful.

I suppose I’ve had passing thoughts, but I wouldn’t say I’m sitting there blaming myself. Mostly I keep thinking about what needs to be handled properly, who needs calling, whether people are being looked after. So… no, not in any clear way, I don’t think.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or on the contrary, have you been more restless or fidgety since your cousin passed away?

I don’t think so. I mean, no one has said I’m talking slower, and believe me, people in my office would comment if I started dragging through a meeting. Although I haven’t exactly been in normal meetings, so maybe that’s not the best measure.

Restless… I’ve been busy, but that’s different, isn’t it? There are always things to arrange, calls to return, people standing around not knowing where the serving spoons are—sorry, that’s not what you asked. I haven’t noticed myself fidgeting or moving strangely, no.
Would you say that most days, your mood has been down or depressed, not just in the moments when you’re thinking about your cousin, but overall throughout the day?

I’m not sure I’d call it depressed overall, no. I mean, there are stretches where everything feels heavy, especially when someone says something kind and you have to stand there and not fall apart in the middle of a room full of people.

But throughout the whole day? I don’t know. I’ve still been doing things, answering messages, making decisions—though half of them are ridiculous little decisions, like whether there’s enough coffee or who’s taking home which dish. So… I wouldn’t say most of the day I’m just down in that way. It comes and goes, I think.
Have you found it harder to think clearly, make decisions, or focus on tasks since your cousin passed away?

I… don’t think so, not in any big way. I mean, I’ve always got a lot of moving pieces in my head, and right now there are more than usual, so if I forget whether I called someone back, that may just be because there are too many calls.

Decisions, though—people keep asking me things, and I can answer. Sometimes I get irritated because it’s like, why are we discussing paper plates for ten minutes? But I don’t think that’s the same as not being able to think clearly. So… no, I haven’t really noticed a major problem with focus or decisions.
Would you say that you’ve completely lost interest in things you used to enjoy, even temporarily, since your cousin passed away?

I don’t know that I’ve completely lost interest, no. I mean, I haven’t exactly been sitting down with a novel or planning dinner with friends, but that feels more like… there hasn’t been room for it.

And honestly, some of the things I usually enjoy feel a little inappropriate right now, if that makes sense. Like I caught myself looking at something online—nothing important, just some ridiculous home renovation thing—and then thought, what am I doing? But I wouldn’t say I can’t enjoy anything or that it’s all gone. It’s just not where my attention is.
Have there been days—more than just a few—where you felt down or emotionally empty most of the day, even when you weren’t thinking about your cousin?

I don’t think so… not more than a few days, no. I mean, there are moments where I feel sort of hollow, but then someone asks where the serving spoons are or whether I approved the program text, and suddenly I’m back in logistics mode.

It’s funny, I used to joke at work that crisis management is just making lists while everyone else panics, and apparently that applies at home too. So emotionally empty most of the day when I’m not thinking about him? I haven’t really noticed that. It’s more like it hits in waves.
Have you had several days in a row where you felt emotionally flat or unable to feel pleasure, even when you weren't thinking about your cousin or being reminded of the loss?

Several days in a row… I’m not sure I’d put it that neatly. But yes, there have been times where I was sort of going through the motions.

At the prayer gatherings, for example, I knew exactly what to do—stand here, thank this person, accept condolences, make sure my aunt had a chair. It’s like hosting an annual board reception, except of course that’s a terrible comparison, sorry. But I was behaving properly, saying the right things, and inside there just wasn’t much warmth.

Even when my nieces tried to comfort me—sweet girls, and they meant it—I remember thinking I should feel some relief or tenderness, and it was more like that affectionate part of me had gone quiet. Not forever, I don’t think. But in those moments, yes, flat.
Have you had several days in a row where you felt down or depressed most of the day, even when you weren’t thinking about your cousin or the loss?

I’m not sure I’d call it depressed most of the day, several days in a row. I mean, I’ve had low stretches, certainly, but it’s hard to separate them from everything happening around me.

Most days have been so full of tasks—calls, food, people coming by—that I don’t really sit still long enough to measure my mood, if that makes sense. It reminds me of when we were preparing for a merger and everyone kept asking how I was sleeping, and I thought, who has time to notice? Sorry, that’s not exactly what you asked.

So… no, I don’t think I’ve noticed being down all day like that when I’m not thinking about him. It’s more mixed than that.
